subtype: Ill teen feeling foggy and cranky [Actor]
passage: In their village near Satara, Samir lay under two blankets, aching, while the cricket tournament's loudspeaker crackled from the school ground. "I'm quitting the team," he croaked when Rajni brought rice kanji. "They'll drop me anyway. And I'm leaving tuition. What's the point?" He glared at the ceiling, then at her. "And stop checking on me!" Rajni set the bowl down. "You can decide all that. Just not today. Your head is full of fever. Big decisions can wait till you can stand without wobbling." "But the board exams, I'm missing classes..." "Sunita will bring notes. Today your only job is rest." She added quietly that if the fever kept going or worried them, they would take the bus to the doctor in town. The next week Samir was back on the ground, bowling badly and grinning. He never mentioned quitting.

qa.q: What did Rajni bring Samir?
qa.a: Rice kanji.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling as he lay in bed?
qa.a: He felt achy, cranky and hopeless, and worried about the team and missing classes.

qa.q: What was wise about Rajni's reply?
qa.a: She did not argue but put big decisions off until Samir recovered, since fever dulls thinking and mood.

qa.q: How might Rajni have felt when Samir snapped at her to stop checking?
qa.a: She may have felt a little hurt, but she stayed calm because she saw it was the illness talking.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager with flu feeling heavy and short-tempered and wanting to make big decisions, and a parent asking him to wait until he recovers.

subtype: Ill teen feeling foggy and cranky [Actor]
passage: The debate final was on Friday, rain had flooded the road to school, and Tanuja had a fever that made her whole body feel packed in wet sand. On Thursday night she sat up in bed with her notes and snapped at Binita Didi for bringing soup. "I'm not missing it. I'll be fine." She read the same paragraph five times. Then she typed a furious message to her debate partner about changing the whole opening argument, and stopped with her thumb over send. Didi sat on the bed. "You can't think straight with this fever. Don't decide anything tonight. Sleep, and we'll see in the morning." In the morning Tanuja's head still felt stuffed with cotton. She deleted the message, called her partner, and asked the reserve speaker to take her place.

qa.q: How many times did Tanuja read the same paragraph?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: What was Tanuja worried about on Thursday night?
qa.a: She was anxious about missing the debate final, and cranky enough to snap at Binita Didi.

qa.q: Why was leaving the decision till morning sensible?
qa.a: The fever was dulling her thinking and mood, so waiting stopped a rash message and let her choose calmly to rest.

qa.q: How might Binita Didi feel when snapped at over the soup?
qa.a: Stung but understanding, since she knew the fever was talking, and she still stayed to help.

grounding: Shows a teen with flu feeling foggy and short-tempered and worried about missing school events, and big decisions being left until she recovers.

subtype: Ill teen feeling foggy and cranky [Actor]
passage: Naveen had been in bed with flu for three days in their Chennai flat, and his thoughts felt as if they were wading through syrup. When Karthik called about the group project, Naveen listened to his idea of changing the topic and exploded. "Fine, do whatever you want. I don't care about the stupid project!" He hung up and threw the phone onto the blanket. Ten minutes later he was staring at the ceiling, ashamed and worried: what if the others dropped him? What if he failed the term? His mother brought him rasam and found him close to tears. "You're sick, kanna. Everything looks worse right now. Don't settle anything today." The next evening, feeling a little better, he called Karthik back. "Sorry about yesterday. Your topic's actually good. Can we talk properly when I'm back?"

qa.q: How long had Naveen been in bed with flu?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel staring at the ceiling after hanging up?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and anxious, worried the group would drop him and he would fail the term.

qa.q: What made the second call go better?
qa.a: Waiting until he felt better meant he could think clearly, apologise, and see that Karthik's topic was good.

qa.q: How might Karthik have felt when Naveen hung up?
qa.a: Karthik was probably hurt and confused, having only suggested an idea.

grounding: Shows a teen with flu feeling foggy, cranky and anxious about school, and learning to leave arguments and decisions until recovery.

passage:
"Mamma, I have to go to school. The maths test is tomorrow."
Madhuri sat on the edge of the bed. "Tanuja, you have a fever, and you've slept all afternoon."
"I'll be fine! If I miss it, I'll have to do the retest, and everyone will think I'm faking."
"Nobody will think that."
"You don't know! Ugh, why are you always like this?"
"Like what?"
"I don't know. Everything's annoying. My head is full of fog."
"That's the flu talking. Your brain is tired too."
"But what about the test?"
"Here's the deal. No big decisions tonight. You rest. In the morning, if you still feel this bad, I'll email Mrs Iyer about the retest."
"Okay. Can you sit with me a bit?"
"Of course. I'm not going anywhere."

qa.a: The maths test is tomorrow.

qa.q: What was Tanuja worried about?
qa.a: Tanuja was anxious about missing the test and afraid everyone would think it was faked.

qa.q: Why is Madhuri's "no big decisions tonight" plan wise?
qa.a: Illness fogs thinking and mood, so deciding about the test in the morning, and asking the teacher, is calmer than arguing now.

qa.q: How does Madhuri take the snap "why are you always like this?"
qa.a: Madhuri doesn't take it personally, seeing it as the flu talking.

grounding: Shows a teen with flu feeling foggy, cranky and worried about missing a test, and a parent postponing decisions until recovery.

subtype: Ill teen feeling foggy and cranky [Actor]
passage: Last month I had flu for a week, and I've never felt so stupid. My body felt like wet sand. I tried to revise for the unit test from bed and read the same paragraph ten times. Then I started worrying I'd fail and fall behind forever. When my brother Suraj came in to ask about his cricket bat, I screamed at him and threw a pillow. Ammi made me put the books away. 'Your brain is sick too, Farida. Decide nothing, argue nothing, just rest.' I slept for two days. The test got moved, and I apologised to Suraj once I could think again. His bat was under my bed.

qa.q: Where was Suraj's cricket bat?
qa.a: Under the bed.

qa.q: What was Farida worried about while ill?
qa.a: Farida felt anxious about failing the unit test and falling behind forever.

qa.q: What did Ammi advise, and why was it wise?
qa.a: To decide nothing, argue nothing and just rest, because illness dulls thinking and mood.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt when the pillow flew at him?
qa.a: He probably felt shocked and hurt, since he had only asked about his bat.

grounding: A teenager with flu feels foggy and short-tempered and worries about school, and learns to leave decisions and arguments until recovery.
